analysis.one_liner: Phases out nonessential uses of "forever chemicals" and bans their release into the environment.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2024 and referred to five House committees, but never advanced past a subcommittee referral and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required companies to stop making and using "forever chemicals" (PFAS) for nonessential purposes within 10 years, with faster bans on PFAS in products like carpets, food packaging, cosmetics, and clothing. It would also have made it illegal to release PFAS into the environment at detectable levels after 10 years, with fines and criminal penalties, allowed citizens to sue polluters, and opened the door for people exposed to PFAS to sue for damages under state law. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to PFAS through drinking water, food packaging, clothing, and contaminated communities, since the bill would have cut off the chemicals at the source and given communities notice and lawsuit rights when endangerment occurs. Public water systems and treatment plants were explicitly exempted from liability as mere receivers of PFAS.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to PFAS through water and products

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers and users of PFAS to report annually on their essential uses, safer alternatives, and any environmental releases, with reports published for public comment.
Bans nonessential PFAS uses within 10 years, with faster bans on PFAS in carpets, food packaging, cosmetics, furniture, apparel, and oil and gas products.
After 10 years, makes it illegal to release any detectable quantity of PFAS into the environment, enforceable with civil and criminal penalties.
Lets citizens sue manufacturers and even federal agencies over PFAS violations, and waives federal immunity so government facilities must follow the same PFAS laws as anyone else.
Makes it easier for people harmed by PFAS exposure to win damages under state law and closes a bankruptcy maneuver that chemical company defendants have used to avoid liability.

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers and the companies that use the chemicals in consumer products, who would bear phaseout, reporting, and fee costs, plus potential liability for past releases and exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS makers and manufacturers using them

drawbacks.text: The blanket ban on releasing PFAS above detection levels after 10 years could be technically difficult to meet for essential uses, since PFAS are so widespread and persistent that even trace releases might be unavoidable in some processes.

The bill would impose significant reporting, phaseout-plan, and fee costs on manufacturers and users of PFAS, which could be passed through to consumers as higher prices for affected goods, even though reduced fees were allowed for small manufacturers.

Removing PFAS from products like waterproof outdoor apparel and some medical or industrial equipment could impose transition costs and performance trade-offs during the decade-long phaseout, particularly until safer alternatives were proven.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and cleanup benefits are large: PFAS exposure is linked to cancer, liver and immune harm, and the bill's phaseout, release ban, and legal-liability provisions would cut exposure and shift cleanup costs to polluters. The costs are also real: some products (rain gear, medical devices, certain industrial processes) currently depend on PFAS, and a 10-year deadline plus liability exposure could raise prices or disrupt supply chains before alternatives fully exist — a trade-off the bill manages through essential-use designations and a research exception but not perfectly. The main weakness is not design but fate: it never received even a subcommittee hearing, so its provisions were never tested in markup.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees and then a subcommittee, and no committee ever acted on it before the congressional session ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Betty McCollum introduced the bill on April 18, 2024, joined by Rep. Chellie Pingree as the sole cosponsor.

The Speaker referred it to five committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Oversight, Science, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Armed Services — a multi-committee referral that makes passage harder because each committee must act on its share.
On April 26, 2024, the part under Energy and Commerce jurisdiction was sent to its Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials Subcommittee, where it stayed.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, as all unpassed bills do.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical manufacturers and PFAS-using product makers, who avoided a mandatory phaseout, release ban, and expanded liability.

for.name: Rep. Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out nonessential PFAS uses and prohibit PFAS releases.

for.name: Rep. Chellie Pingree
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: PFAS manufacturers and major PFAS-using industries
against.role: Chemical and consumer-product sectors affected by phaseout mandates
against.what_they_did: No record in the provided sources shows a specific actor stopping the bill; it simply was never scheduled for committee or floor action, so no named opponent appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and its only supporters on the record were two Democratic House members, so no party split was ever tested.

industries.note: The bill would force a 10-year phaseout of nonessential PFAS production, ban detectable releases, and expose companies to citizen suits and expanded state-law damages claims. It also blocks the bankruptcy tactic used to escape contamination liability.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers using PFAS (carpets, textiles, cosmetics, food packaging, outdoor apparel)
industries.note: One- to five-year sales bans on PFAS-containing versions of these products would force reformulation or removal from store shelves, with resale of used goods exempted.
PFAS-containing oil and gas products would be banned within one year, hitting a sector that uses PFAS in equipment and operations; the public bears the contamination cost today.

industries.industry: Environmental remediation, testing, and water treatment industry
industries.note: The bill directs federal funding and research through Centers of Excellence for PFAS detection and remediation, establishing a permanent public role for these firms and institutions.
